author: ValWood
body:
hmm, 


Claude
Yes, the core findings described in that passage — which come from a 2018 paper on yeast KEOPS and telomere regulation — remain broadly supported by subsequent research. Here's a summary of where things stand:
The original findings hold up well in S. cerevisiae. The key claim that KEOPS regulates telomere length via a t6A-independent mechanism has been corroborated by follow-up work. A 2019 study in Nucleic Acids Research independently replicated the Qri7 complementation approach and confirmed that while cytoplasmic expression of Qri7 fully rescues slow growth and t6A defects in KEOPS mutants, it does not rescue telomere shortening [Oxford Academic](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/47/11/5684/5425341), reinforcing the conclusion that the telomere function is separable from tRNA modification activity.
The t6A-independent theme has since been extended. That same 2019 study further revealed that KEOPS plays positive roles in both DNA damage response and homologous recombination-mediated DNA repair, independently of its t6A synthesis function, with the complex displaying direct DNA binding activity and being recruited to chromatin at DNA breaks [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30937455/). This broadens the picture of KEOPS as having multiple chromatin-related functions beyond tRNA modification.
The picture is more nuanced in other fungi. Interestingly, work in Cryptococcus neoformans suggests the telomere-regulation role of KEOPS is not universally conserved. Research in C. neoformans found that while the KEOPS complex conserves its roles in t6A modification and transcriptional regulation, the telomere regulation function appears absent [ASM Journals](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/mbio.02944-22) in that organism, implying evolutionary divergence in how KEOPS functions have been partitioned.
The mechanistic picture remains incomplete. One important open question from the original paper — exactly how KEOPS promotes G-overhang generation at telomeres in a t6A-independent manner — still lacks a fully resolved molecular mechanism. The KEOPS complex's DNA binding capacity is increasingly seen as relevant, but the precise pathway connecting it to telomerase or resection machinery at telomeres in yeast is still an active area of investigation.
So in short: yes, the model holds, and has been reinforced and extended — but the precise molecular mechanism of the t6A-independent telomere function remains an open question.

So maybe it is relevant, but it could also be very indirect, and may not be conserved. One issue is that mutations in many unrelated processes can cause a telomere elongation phenotype.
